extracted.intended_audience: advocates, grassroots organizers, affected individuals, and public-interest lawyers interested in using notice-and-comment (especially on Medicaid Section 1115 waivers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using the administrative notice-and-comment process as an advocacy tool—how and why to submit comments (particularly on Medicaid Section 1115 waiver proposals), who should comment, and what kinds of content are valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in notice-and-comment even under deregulatory administrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment remains a key tool even in an anti-regulatory moment; under the Administrative Procedure Act, agencies sometimes must solicit public comments when changing course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume there is nothing to comment on simply because an administration favors deregulation. Monitor agency actions because some changes (e.g., delaying or altering rules, approving waivers) trigger APA notice-and-comment obligations. Example: Department of Education’s delay of a 2016 regulation drew more than 300 commenters; litigation followed. Anti-pattern: ignoring opportunities to comment because one expects an administration to be unreceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft comments with judicial impact in mind (create a record for courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should be written partly because 'it will make a difference in court'—public comments become part of the administrative record and can be relied on in judicial challenges to agency actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, frame comments so they document harms, demonstrate inconsistency with statutory/regulatory requirements, and supply evidentiary material that a reviewing court could find persuasive. Cite examples where comments contributed to judicial outcomes (e.g., Stewart v. Azar vacating an HHS waiver). Anti-pattern: treating comments only as symbolic protest without supplying factual detail that could support legal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilize and affirm 'grassroots experts' by centering firsthand practitioner knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: One value of commenting is mobilizing communities of 'grassroots experts'—counselors, home health aides, advocates, and others with deep practical knowledge who lack powerful professional organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage and support people with lived or professional experience to submit comments describing the realities they see. Community-based commenting both produces useful content and affirms contributors' expertise. Practical step: organize and educate peers on how to write and submit comments. Anti-pattern: privileging only high-credential voices while overlooking practitioner testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a public record (archive) of the human toll through personal testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments create a public record—an archive—of the human consequences of governmental choices, preserving stories of harm for public and legal audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include personal stories and detailed anecdotes that illustrate concrete harms (e.g., loss of benefits, relapse due to lost medication, loss of custody, resorting to unsafe alternatives). Such testimony helps historians, courts, and future advocates assess the human impact. Anticipate agency dismissal of emotive accounts as 'hyperbole,' but recognize that different audiences may weigh them differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include concrete, specific details about burdens and barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comments document concrete realities—unpredictable earnings, inaccessible transportation, unaffordable child care, burdensome documentary requirements, and other barriers that show how proposed changes operate on the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples (dates, procedural steps, administrative actions, specific outcomes) and connect them to how a proposed rule or waiver would increase harm. Examples in the post: MaineCare termination for misplaced documentation, people buying pet antibiotics, or being unable to afford medication. Anti-pattern: vague denunciations without factual anchors that tie harms to the policy change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor/flag agency proposals and provide/how-to guidance to peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Active monitoring and rapid dissemination (flagging) of agency requests for comment helps mobilize responses; accompanying how-to guidance increases participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up systems or networks to spot waiver requests (e.g., 1115 waivers), notify communities, and circulate simple guides on how to submit comments. The authors reference existing resources such as 'Notice and Comment 101' (Know Your IX) and the Public Comment Project how-to guide, and Cortland’s own guides on writing comments. Anti-pattern: leaving the discovery and submission process opaque and centralized among a few actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use moral and emotional framing strategically despite possible administrative dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotive moral language (e.g., claims that a policy 'will kill people') may be dismissed by agency officials as hyperbole, but it can register with other audiences (judges, the public, historians) and underscore the stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance moral/emotional claims with concrete facts and testimony so that strong language is anchored in documented harms. Recognize multiple audiences: an agency might reject emotive testimony, but courts or the public may find it persuasive as evidence of consequence or intent. Anti-pattern: relying solely on moralizing rhetoric without documentary or factual support.
